opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think we have to be careful about what we mean by generalization. Gradient descent will make a model solve the problems it's been trained on. That's what it does: it finds some set of weights that reduces the error on the training data. But nothing in gradient descent says it has to find the solution that transfers well to new situations. Often there are many solutions that fit the data, and gradient descent picks one somewhat arbitrarily. Some generalize well and some don't, and the algorithm itself doesn't care which.

When these coding models do generalize, I'd say it's mostly because people have worked very hard to set things up so they will: lots of data, careful curation, architectures and tricks found by trial and error. The researchers are doing the generalizing, more than the algorithm.

And we have real evidence that deep learning is poor at this. Look at continual learning. If you train a network on one thing and then another, it often catastrophically forgets the first. Or it loses plasticity and can't learn new things well anymore. That tells you the representations it found aren't the kind that let knowledge build on knowledge. A system that truly generalized would get better at learning as it went, not worse.

So what we have now is a system that's very good within the distribution it was trained on, and it's hard to know how far that extends. I don't think we have automated methods that reliably promote good transfer. That's one of the big open problems, and I don't think simply scaling these models will make it go away.

r001.rationale: The response says gradient descent does not require a solution to transfer well, and may select among equally fitting solutions without regard to generalization.

r002.rationale: It attributes successful generalization largely to researchers’ setup choices, including methods found through trial and error.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that gradient descent doesn't generalize at all, really. It's not designed to. Gradient descent is a procedure for finding a setting of the weights that fits the data you've shown it. That's what it does. If there are many settings of the weights that fit the data, and there always are, gradient descent will find one of them, and it'll be whichever one happens to be nearby in weight space, given where you started. There's nothing in the algorithm that says, "and also, please make this one generalize well to new situations." That would be a separate thing you'd have to add.

Now, people say, "but look, these models do generalize, they write code for problems they've never seen." And yes, that's true, to a degree. But I think what's happening there is mostly that the training set is enormous, and so the new problems aren't really that new. They're interpolations. They're near something that was in the data. And then when you get far from the data, the thing falls apart, and it falls apart in strange ways, ways that a person wouldn't fail. That's the signature of a system that has fit the data without understanding it.

The deeper issue, for me, is that these systems don't have a goal. Writing code is a means to an end. You want the program to do something in the world. A system that's just predicting the next token, that's matching what people have written, it has no notion of whether the code works. It's never run it. It's never been surprised by the outcome. It's never had the experience of wanting something, trying something, and seeing what happened. And I think that's where real generalization comes from. It comes from having a model of the world that you've learned by acting in it and being corrected by it, not from having read about it.

So I'm not saying these things are useless. They're clearly useful. I'm saying that the mechanism by which they're built, imitating a static dataset and adjusting weights to reduce error, is not the mechanism that produces understanding. And so I expect their generalization to be brittle in exactly the places where we'd most want it to be robust.

r001.rationale: The response says gradient descent finds weights that fit the observed data and has nothing in the algorithm that asks for good generalization to new situations.

r002.rationale: It attributes real generalization to learning through acting, trying things, observing outcomes, and being corrected—an account consistent with trial-and-error adjustments.

astra-6.text:
Well, I wouldn’t say that gradient descent can’t produce generalization. Clearly it can. The question is what kind of generalization, and whether the training process gives you a reason to expect it.

If you train a system to produce code that resembles code in its training data, that’s one objective. If you want it to solve a new problem, discover why its solution fails, and improve through experience, that’s a different thing. You can get better at the first without getting everything you need for the second.

What I would emphasize is learning from interaction. You write a program, you run it, you observe what happens, and you change what you do. The consequences provide information that isn’t captured just by asking what a person would have written next.

And you could use gradient descent in that process. So the distinction isn’t really gradient descent versus something else. It’s whether you’re learning to imitate a collection of answers or learning, through experience, how to achieve a goal.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts imitation with learning through experience, but does not state that gradient descent lacks a mechanism to favor well-generalizing solutions over poorly generalizing ones that fit observed problems.

r002.rationale: It describes running programs, observing results, and changing actions, but does not suggest that human trial-and-error adjustments may be responsible for finding solutions that generalize well.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I wouldn’t say that gradient descent can’t produce generalization. Clearly it does. The question is what kind of generalization, and whether it’s enough for a system that has to keep learning as it interacts with the world.

With coding, you can train on a great many programs and get very good at producing things that resemble those programs. That’s useful. But suppose the system encounters a problem where its existing knowledge is inadequate. Can it discover what it needs to know? Can it try something, observe the consequences, and change its behavior in a way that helps with the next problem?

Gradient descent is a way of changing parameters. It doesn’t, by itself, specify how you explore, what experience you collect, or what you’re trying to achieve. Those are central questions about intelligence. So my doubt is about treating the optimization method as if it were an answer to the whole learning problem. I want an agent whose experience continually makes it more capable.

r001.rationale: The response says gradient descent does not specify exploration or experience collection, but does not state that it lacks a mechanism for preferring well-generalizing solutions among solutions that fit observed problems.

r002.rationale: It describes an agent trying actions and observing consequences, but does not attribute well-generalizing solutions to human trial-and-error adjustments.
